content.text: Claude Code ends its turn when the work looks done. If it has nothing to run that comes back pass or fail, "looks done" is all it can go on, and you become the test suite. Give it a check, such as tests, a typecheck or a build, and ask for the output; when the check must pass every time, enforce it with a Stop hook.

A developer asks Claude Code to add a promo code field to the checkout form. A minute later: "Done. Added the field, the validation and the API call, and updated the order total." The diff reads well, so it gets pushed. CI fails: the order summary component still passes the old total shape, and a pricing test expects two decimal places. Nothing in the session ever ran the tests or the typechecker. Claude didn't lie. It stopped when the work looked done, and nothing told it otherwise.
The common misconception
"When Claude Code says the task is done, the change works, so there's no need for tests or another check." It's an easy belief to fall into:

items.text: The summary is specific and confident. It lists files, functions and edge cases, and reads like a report of verified work.
It's often right. Anthropic's docs say that in most cases a plain first prompt in a fresh session already does the right thing.
Claude Code's own loop has a "verify results" phase, so it's natural to assume verification always happens.
The diff looks right, and reading a diff feels like checking it.

content.text: The half-truth: Claude does verify when it has a way to. Its loop is gather context, take action, verify results. But verifying needs something that returns pass or fail. Without that, Claude's judgment that the work looks right is the whole verification step.
What actually happens
Claude stops when the work looks done

The docs put it plainly: "Claude stops when the work looks done." With nothing to run, "In practice that makes you the test suite, and every mistake sits there until you happen to notice it." They list this among the four usual reasons a session goes wrong: Claude said it was done and it wasn't quite, "usually because it had no way to check its own work."
A check closes the loop

Give Claude something that comes back pass or fail, and it closes the loop itself: it makes the change, runs the check, reads the output if something broke, fixes it and runs the check again. The check can be almost anything whose result Claude can read:

items.text: A test file, or a build's exit code
A script that diffs output against a fixture
A browser screenshot next to the mockup

content.text: Who decides it's done
The docs sort every instruction into two kinds. Non-deterministic ones are read by the model, which decides what to do with them: your prompt, a
CLAUDE.md
line, a skill. Deterministic ones are applied by Claude Code, the harness, every time: hooks, deny rules, managed settings. "Done" comes in both kinds, at four levels of strictness:

rows.text: "Run the tests and keep going until they pass" in the prompt
A separate small, fast model, after every turn
Your script's exit code, run by Claude Code
A fresh subagent that never saw the conversation

content.text: /goal

deserves a closer look. Its evaluator gets the condition and the conversation so far; it doesn't run commands or read files. So "all tests in test/auth pass" works because Claude runs the tests and the result shows up in the transcript. A condition such as "the checkout works" gives the evaluator nothing to check.
Ask for evidence, not a verdict

Whichever option you choose, ask Claude for the command it ran and its output, or the screenshot. The docs are direct: "All tests pass" on its own tells you very little, and reading the output is faster than rerunning the check yourself. For a session you weren't watching, it's the only evidence you have.
Same task, with and without a check

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# No check: Claude stops when the diff looks right
claude "Add a promo code field to the checkout form"

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# A check, a finish line and a request for evidence
claude "Add a promo code field to the checkout form. Then run
pnpm vitest run src/checkout and pnpm tsc --noEmit, keep going
until both pass, and paste the final output."

content.text: The second prompt costs two extra sentences. It defines "done" as commands Claude can run, and it gives you output to read instead of a summary to trust.
Enforcing the check with a Stop hook
A line such as "Always typecheck before you finish", in a prompt or in CLAUDE.md, works most of the time, not every time. When the check must pass before every stop, make it a
Stop hook

The hook runs whenever Claude tries to end its turn. Exit code 2 blocks the stop, and whatever the command prints to stderr goes back to Claude as the reason it can't finish yet; that's why the compiler output is redirected with
. To test it, ask for a change that breaks a type: instead of finishing, Claude gets the compiler errors and keeps going until
tsc
passes.

blocks.title: The most useful line in your CLAUDE.md

content.text: If your repo already has a check, the docs call the command that runs it "the single most useful line" in CLAUDE.md. Add the command for one test file too, such as
pnpm vitest run path/to/file.test.ts
, so Claude can check a small change without running the whole suite.

blocks.title: A check that can never pass

content.text: A Stop hook that keeps failing doesn't block forever. After it blocks eight times in a row with no tool call from Claude in between, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn. If the check depends on something Claude can't fix, such as a missing
DATABASE_URL
, the turn ends red after wasted work. The hook's input includes
stop_hook_active
, which is
true
when Claude is already continuing because of a stop hook; a script can check it and let Claude stop.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find the check you already have

content.text: Tests, a typecheck, a linter, a build. If there's nothing yet, a small script that diffs output against a fixture counts.
Write the exact test, typecheck and lint commands, plus how to run a single test file. Only the commands: enforcing them is a hook's job.
Name the check, tell Claude to keep going until it passes, and ask for the final output rather than a summary.

items.title: Enforce the non-negotiable check with a Stop hook

content.text: Commit it in
.claude/settings.json
so it applies to everyone who works in the repo. Keep it fast, because it runs every time Claude tries to stop.
For long or background work, state one measurable end state and how to prove it, and add a limit such as
or stop after 20 turns
Key takeaways

items.text: Claude stops when the work looks done; without a check, "looks done" is all it has to go on.
A check is anything that comes back pass or fail: tests, a typecheck, a linter, a build, a fixture diff.
Prompt and CLAUDE.md lines are followed most of the time; a Stop hook is enforced by Claude Code every time.
's evaluator reads the conversation and runs nothing, so the proof must appear in the transcript.
Ask for the command and its output, not for "all tests pass".
